alts.name: Argentina (the Hirsch colonies, from 1891)
facts: In Der Judenstaat (14 Feb 1896) Herzl named two possible lands, Argentina and Palestine. Both, he wrote, would fail by slow "infiltration": immigration was pointless without a sovereign right to keep it going.
a_wp_judenstaat

Baron Maurice de Hirsch founded the Jewish Colonization Association in 1891 to move Jews out of the Russian Empire and settle them as farmers in Argentina; he spent nearly his whole fortune on it. At his death in 1896 there were 6,757 colonists.
a_wp_hirsch_arg

By 1923 the Association had settled 30,725 people (5,360 families) on 590,000 hectares, more than three times all the land Jews held in Palestine on the eve of statehood (about 173,000 hectares, of which the JNF held 936,000 dunams).
a_jta_ica24; a_wp_jnf

The colonies peaked at over 20,000 colonists in 1930. Progress was "hampered by insufficient land for extensive cultivation and the unfavorable location of many of the colonies"; by 1966 only 8,000 Jews remained in them.
a_jvl_ica
Argentina was an independent republic that welcomed European immigrants as citizens. No Argentine government offered self-rule to the colonies, and none was sought.
a_wp_judenstaat; a_wp_hirsch_arg

January 1919, the Tragic Week in Buenos Aires: during the suppression of a general strike the Argentine Patriotic League singled out the Jewish neighborhood of Once, in what has been called the first pogrom in the Americas.
a_jc_tragic

money: Hirsch's fortune went to Argentina; nothing documented of the movement's later money (Edmond, the Keren Hayesod, the American appeals) would have.
land: More land was bought than in all of Palestine; land was not the limit.
force: No armed body: the colonists were citizens under Argentine law.
diplomacy: No sovereign willing to grant self-rule; Herzl's own condition, a sovereign right, never met.
organization: The Association organized settlement, but the Zionist Organization never adopted Argentina.
recognition: No international process toward a state.

alts.path: A large community of citizens, not a state. That is what happened: farm colonies of up to 20,000 people, most of whose children moved to the cities, inside a Jewish community that became one of the largest in the Americas.
alts.cost: No war over sovereignty, because sovereignty never changed hands. There was violence against Jews all the same (the 1919 Tragic Week).

alts.name: British East Africa, the "Uganda" offer (1903)
facts: After the Kishinev pogrom, Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain offered land for Jewish settlement in British East Africa: about 16,300 square kilometres of the Uasin Gishu plateau, in what is now Kenya, between Lake Nakuru, Kisumu and Mount Elgon. That is smaller than Mandatory Palestine (about 26,000 square kilometres).
a_ea_kenya; a_wp_mandpal

26 Aug 1903: the Sixth Zionist Congress voted 295 to 178 only to send a commission to look at it. Herzl presented it as a temporary refuge for Jews in danger in Russia, not a replacement for the Land of Israel.
a_jvl_uganda; a_ea_kenya
The three-man commission split two to one against it.
a_ea_kenya
British settlers opposed the plan; the East African Standard denounced "pauper alien Jews" turning the highlands into "Jewganda".
a_ea_kenya

The plateau was Maasai grazing land. Under agreements of 1904 and 1911 the British moved the Maasai off much of the Rift Valley and the Uasin Gishu to make room for European settlers; over a million acres had been leased or sold by the end of 1905.
a_unpo_maasai; a_ea_kenya

The Seventh Zionist Congress rejected the offer in 1905. Israel Zangwill led the minority out and founded the Jewish Territorial Organization, which searched for a territory elsewhere (Angola, Galveston and others), found none, and dissolved in 1925; in 1944 Australia vetoed the last such plan, in the Kimberley.
a_wp_ito

money: The large sums of the record were raised for Palestine; nothing documented would have followed to East Africa.
land: Land offered by the ruling power without purchase, but smaller than Palestine and judged unsuitable by the commission.
force: British protection, but no Jewish force and settler hostility.
diplomacy: The ruling power made the offer itself; the settlers and the Protectorate's officials opposed it.
organization: The movement approved only a survey, split over it, and rejected it in 1905.
recognition: At most a self-governing settlement under the British crown; no route to statehood on the record.

alts.path: At most a small self-governing settlement under British rule, opposed by the British settlers, on land taken from the Maasai. On the record the movement itself refused it, and those who did go looking for a territory found no ruler willing to give one.
alts.cost: Not a peaceful alternative: the land was already the Maasai's, and its settlers fought for it.

palestine.name: Palestine (the record)
facts: About 25,600 to 26,600 square kilometres; in 1945 about 1,061,000 Muslims, 136,000 Christians and 554,000 Jews.
a_wp_mandpal

The two sides' positions were an "irreconcilable conflict of principles", Bevin told the Commons on 18 February 1947: the Jews sought a sovereign state, and the Arabs opposed Jewish sovereignty anywhere in Palestine.
a_cojs_47
palestine.path: The state, founded in 1948, through war.
palestine.cost: A war in 1947-49 and a conflict that has continued since.
